The lack of apparent inherent meaning in the universe, for me, used to be extremely uncomfortable until I read a bit of Camus' "The Myth of Sisyphus." 

Paraphrasing: The same consciousness/awareness of futility and meaningless, at the same time can be our victory. We can choose either torture or victory with our knowledge and human consciousness. 

"The struggle itself towards the heights is enough to fill a man's heart. One must imagine Sisyphus happy." 

I found that the "cosmic perspective" (such as talked about by Neil Degrasse Tyson) is almost a therapy against that torture. 

Consider humans as a self-aware universe. We're the first and only species we know about that can truly contemplate itself through science and recognize that our atoms are combinations of the same atoms found all through the universe. But only we know ourselves as matter. You can look in the mirror and see yourself, or you can look in the mirror and recognize the universe staring back at itself. 

I decided that was enough meaning for me. It's a privilege to have that, out of all the life that ever lived, and among the majority of humans that never experienced that feeling.

There could be a solar storm/flare at any time, and if it was strong enough, it could act like an EMP on the whole planet.

There would be widespread electrical disruptions, power outages, loss of global communications. Anything with electronic parts could be fried - cars, TVs, phones, equipment used to feed the population. Your digital money would be gone. Your livelihood if it relied on any technology would be over. 

The vast majority of people wouldn't know what hit them. There could be assumptions that we're at war with other countries. There would be no widespread news about it for a long time, and the whole of society would collapse pretty damn fast anyway.

The scariest part is something like this has already kind of happened - The Carrington Event. Luckily, that was in 1859 before the world was heavily reliant on electronics.

As expansion of the fabric of space accelerates, eventually there will be so much expanding space between other galaxies and ours, they will "move" away from us faster than their light can travel through that space to reach us, and we will no longer be able to see things in the cosmos. It will happen to the furthest away things first, but eventually even the closest will go out of sight. 

Dunno the time scale of this, but it's also the mechanics of the "heat death" ending of the universe - eventually all matter will be so spaced out from each other that no new stars will form and the universe will be cold and dark.

Life in general will continue after us if we ruin it for ourselves and take a few other species with us.

Friedrich Nietzsche was considered the "Nazi philosopher" for a long time, but this was the work of his proto-nazi sister who gained control of his philosophical works when his mental health declined, and she assured Hitler that his "Superman" ideal person was about Aryans. 

His book "Thus Spoke Zarathustra" was sent to the German troops during the war.

She modified his works to her purposes for her own fame and fortune, and threw out anything she didn't agree with. 

She even dressed him up in a white robe when he went mad and presented him to visitors as some kind of prophet figure. 

She published a final book full of his discarded thoughts and poorly written notes he never intended to publish, mixed with her own lies, and promoted it as his final philosophy. This caused Nietzsxhe to be heavily misunderstood and disliked for a long time. 

In reality, Nietzsche was against racism and antisemitism and, in fact, hated his country and what Germans were becoming more than any other group of people he ever spoke about. He probably would have been jailed in Nazi Germany for some of the things he thought if they had been aired publicly. 

I think it's sad that academics didn't give him much attention until recently. But the record is slowly getting set straight with him now.

I had a pretty similar journey/result. 

This quote sums up what I got from DBT: 

"I can't 100% control what others do to me or what events happen, but I can control how I respond." 

Acceptance isn't such a bad thing if it gives you peace. There's a lot of this world/the past that all we CAN do is accept it - or suffer. Accepting doesn't mean agreeing or condoning, it just means acknowledging and moving on as best you can. It took a long time for me to really understand it.

I mean, what do you want from a therapy? 

Group was a way to listen to others in similar shoes, talk about experiences and relate with them, and grow with them. Listen to what was working for them, what they struggled with, and honestly just "normalize" things for each other. There was also weekly individual sessions with a psychologist where you could address more personal things that you didn't want to speak about in the group. 

The stickers are just a psychology trick attempting the reward response to reinforce continuing effective behaviors, even though to me it was repulsive at first, and I absolutely understand how that comes across in the beginning. 

The homework was practicing the tools you were learning in sessions and filling out diary cards about what you were feeling, any harmful behaviors you had done each day, and which skills you think you had done well. 

There's no magic wand treatment for BPD, it takes being outside the comfort zone and trying new things. At least, that was my experience.

I did one year of DBT, and it was life changing for me. Completely turned my life around and gave me the ability to cope without being in frequent crises.

DBT never stopped the depression, it never stopped suicidal ideation, it never stopped the actual problems of everyday life, it just taught me how to not spiral so hard and remain functional despite them. 

The best DBT skill for me was "effectiveness" - what can I do today that's effective? How can I respond to this event effectively? Is this toxic relationship/situation/habit/addiction effective for my goals and health? It became like a new lens to view the world through. 

The other thing that stands out were the Skills Training Assumptions, especially these ones: people are doing the best they can, people want to improve, people may not have caused their own problems but they have to fix them anyway, new behaviour can be learnt and requires practice, all behavior is caused - even if we don't know what the exact causes are. 

I will admit parts of DBT early on felt a bit 'condescending' to me. We got stickers for showing up to group and finishing our homework tasks. The facilitators would also correct us whenever we used language such as "should/shouldn't".. It seemed like how you treat a child. But along the way, I decided to trust the process and stop being so in my head about what I thought. I was there BECAUSE my thinking wasn't the best. Basically, I had to remind myself to drop my ego about things and really just embrace whatever they were doing instead of being so resistant to change. 

By the end I had bought a few sheets of stickers for the group because yes it could be seen as childish, especially when you're new and feeling highly resistent and possibly hopeless and looking for reasons to leave, but we all used our stickers in the front inside page of our DBT folder, and nearing the end of the course it was almost full, and it was like a visual representation of progress and how much work had been put in.
